title: A tri-scale in silico framework integrating pharmacovigilance and mechanistic modeling suggests tepotinib-associated acute kidney injury risk

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《A tri-scale in silico framework integrating pharmacovigilance and mechanistic modeling suggests tepotinib-associated acute kidney injury risk》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · S0001-p1】Acute kidney injury (AKI), characterized by a rapid decline in renal function, poses a substantial global health burden due to its high incidence and strong association with poor clinical outcomes [1,2]. In critical care settings, AKI affects more than half of all patients and is independently linked to mortality rates exceeding 50% [3]. The prognostic significance of AKI is further evidenced by its association with increased short-term mortality, even for cases at the lower end of the severity spectrum [4]. A major barrier to effective management is the high rate of underdiagnosis; in large hospital systems, over 70% of AKI cases are missed, leading to delayed interventions and worsened patient prognosis [5–7]. This challenge is particularly acute in oncology. Severe AKI, defined and staged by the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) clinical practice guidelines (corresponding to stage 2 or higher), is a frequent complication among cancer patients, often necessitating renal replacement therapy (RRT) and frequently leading to dose reduction or discontinuation of essential anticancer agents [8,9]. Consequently, the early prediction and prevention of drug-induced AKI have become a critical priority in the clinical management of vulnerable populations such as cancer patients [10,11].

【Introduction · S0001-p2】The expanding arsenal of molecularly targeted therapies has markedly improved oncological outcomes yet simultaneously unveiled a spectrum of organ-specific toxicities, with nephrotoxicity emerging as a no7dose-limiting challenge for several kinase inhibitors (KIs) [12,13]. Tepotinib, a highly selective MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), exemplifies this paradox by demonstrating robust efficacy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with MET alterations, alongside a poorly defined renal safety profile [14]. A critical knowledge gap persists between its well-characterized pulmonary toxicity and the mechanistic obscurity surrounding its potential to induce AKI. Mechanistic insights remain limited as to whether the potential nephrotoxicity of tepotinib originates from on-target MET inhibition or results from promiscuous off-target engagements with kinases vital for renal homeostasis, leaving the implicated apoptotic or inflammatory pathways wholly unexplored [15]. Epidemiologically, the evidence is equally sparse, confined to anecdotal reports without any systematic, large-scale pharmacovigilance analysis to quantify the discrete AKI risk signal in real-world populations [16]. This dual ambiguity—spanning molecular pathogenesis and population-level evidence—significantly impedes the formulation of predictive biomarkers, evidence-based monitoring protocols, and effective risk-mitigation strategies for patients undergoing treatment with this promising agent.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《A tri-scale in silico framework integrating pharmacovigilance and mechanistic modeling suggests tepotinib-associated acute kidney injury risk》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Molecular docking validation · S0002-S2010-p1】In this study, the top six key targets ranked by degree value were selected for molecular docking validation with tepotinib. The SDF structure file of tepotinib was first retrieved from PubChem. Core target protein structures in Protein Data Bank (PDB) format were then downloaded from the RCSB PDB database (https://www.rcsb.org/) using their UniProt IDs. Docking analyses were performed using the CB-Dock2 platform (https://cadd.labshare.cn/cb-dock2/), which integrates CurPocket curvature-based cavity detection with AutoDock Vina. The platform automatically performs ligand and target protein hydrogenation, dehydration, energy optimization, and structure minimization, then identifies large surface cavities as potential binding sites to generate multiple docking conformations. CB-Dock2 selects the docking pose with the lowest Vina score, calculates binding energy, and generates 3D visualizations of binding modes to systematically characterize molecular interactions between tepotinib and core target proteins. These docking results predict potential binding interactions, which serve to prioritize targets for further investigation into functional inhibition.

【Conclusion · S0005-p1】This integrated analysis establishes a significant association between the MET inhibitor tepotinib and AKI. More importantly, it showcases the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline as a reusable, three-scale workflow for evaluating nephrotoxicity across the TKI drug class. Pharmacovigilance mining revealed a robust signal for renal impairment (ROR = 20.60). A convergent multi-scale approach further elucidated the mechanistic basis for this association, pinpointing a toxicity network centered on six hub targets—HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC. These targets dysregulate critical renal pathways, including PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling, an interaction model supported by computational evidence of high-affinity binding from molecular docking. Methodologically, this work presents the first application of the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline, linking FAERS-based signal detection to mechanistic docking via network toxicology. This approach provides a generalizable, hypothesis-generating model to guide future toxicogenomic studies. Consequently, patients receiving tepotinib may benefit from early serum creatinine monitoring and a comprehensive assessment of nephrotoxic risk factors. The FAERS-NetDock Pipeline exemplified here is generalizable for de-risking the development of targeted therapies. This tripartite model can be extended to screen for other off-target organ toxicities, such as cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity or immune-related AEs, in a wide range of targeted oncology agents. As demonstrated with tepotinib, the pipeline is directly applicable for the safety profiling of diverse TKIs, including crizotinib, capmatinib, savolitinib, afatinib, and osimertinib.

sections.title: 图表阅读
sections.text:
《A tri-scale in silico framework integrating pharmacovigilance and mechanistic modeling suggests tepotinib-associated acute kidney injury risk》：图表的原始标题与说明。

【Figure 1. · F0001】Figure 1. Schematic workflow of the integrated in silico framework for assessing tepotinib-related acute kidney injury. The approach progresses from FAERS-based signal detection, through network toxicology analysis for target and pathway identification, to molecular docking validation of hub target binding, thereby establishing a multiscale mechanistic hypothesis.

【Figure 2. · F0002】Figure 2. Workflow of FAERS-based disproportionality analysis for detecting tepotinib-associated acute kidney injury risk.

【Figure 3. · F0003】Figure 3. (a) Venn diagram illustrating the intersection between tepotinib’s potential targets (371, left circle) and AKI-related genes (3,416, right circle), with 173 shared targets identified. Non-overlapping areas: 3,243 AKI-exclusive targets (right) and 198 tepotinib-exclusive targets (left), excluded to prioritize direct drug-disease interactions. (b) Network graph visualizing the complex regulatory relationships of tepotinib (central node) with its key targets (middle-layer nodes) and AKI pathological processes (outer-layer nodes), providing a global perspective for deciphering tepotinib’s multi-target synergistic mechanisms.
